Data Collection

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Data Collection
The indicators and parameters of natural attenuation are monitored for a period of time and the duration of monitoring is specific to each LUFT site. Historically, there has been a belief that natural attenuation requires a long-term monitoring program. Current practical data suggest that, if trends are shown consistently over the course of a year accounting for fluctuations in groundwater elevations, long-term monitoring is not necessary.
Data collection for natural attenuation may not be needed at all of the monitoring well locations at a LUFT site. With the approval of the agency case worker, the select wells and/or specific frequencies can be determined such that the level of data collected is accurate to demonstrate the decreasing trends of COCs, plume stability, etc. Most importantly, monitoring should be conducted only until it has been demonstrated that natural attenuation will continue and eventually meet remedial goals, prior to the resource being needed for a beneficial use, and not for extended periods of time beyond what is needed to establish a data trend.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text: The information in the section is an excerpt from the Monitored Natural Attenuation and Long-Term Monitoring section of the former Air Force Center for Engineering and the Environment (AFCEE) website.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 18-62
Remediation
Chapter 18: Remediation
Remedial Effectiveness
December 1015
After a remedial technology is installed and operational, it is important to determine whether that technology is effective. Generally, declining trends in extracted vapor and/or groundwater are evidence of success.
Declining groundwater concentrations of COCs as compared with data collected before the onset of remediation are evidence of success. Evidence of ineffectiveness includes groundwater concentrations of COCs that persist at or near levels observed before the start of cleanup. Increases in concentrations in wells downgradient from the treatment area may indicate a detrimental effect; for example, incomplete oxidation during ozone sparging. In such cases, the process is promptly stopped to examine potential problems and plan further action.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Exceptions to this generalization include temporary increases in groundwater concentrations in the treatment area shortly after initiation of some forms of remediation. These can be a sign of successful implementation. For example, increases in dissolved-gasoline concentrations after initiation of air sparging in the source area usually represent COCs being stripped from soils below the water table by the sparging process, followed by dissolution in the groundwater. Continued sparging should result in decreasing concentrations over time following the initial “spike” in levels. This effect is also seen during enhanced bioremediation, due to surfactants produced by the microbes as a by-product of metabolism.
For many of these assessments, readily available geographical information systems (GIS) software and simple trend-analysis statistical tools are very useful for data visualization and performance assessment; such tools can enhance data-analysis capabilities.
Further Reading.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Further Reading.
Information from this chapter and further information are available from “Evaluating Remedy Performance” (from Remediation Process Optimization: Identifying Opportunities for Enhanced and More Efficient Site Remediation, 2004, prepared by The Interstate Technology & Regulatory Council [ITRC] Remediation Process Optimization Team).
One of the challenges of effective remediation is determining when remediation is complete. If the RP, in partnership with his/her consultant, does not efficiently manage the endpoint of the remediation process, the lack of operational limits (shutdown criteria) can result in significant, unnecessary costs to both the RP and the UST Cleanup Fund.
In general, once extracted media (vapors, groundwater) or dissolved-plume concentrations decline to stable minimum levels (the third, diffusional stage of extraction), the effective performance limit of the remediation process has been reached. Once it is clear that the remediation system has reached this performance limit, the site’s path forward is revisited with the lead agency.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
If the remediation system performance limit is reached and concentrations remain above remediation goals after verification testing, potential options to be discussed with the regulatory case worker may include • Installation of a new remediation system with different performance goals, • Risk modeling of remaining concentrations in lieu of further physical treatment, and/or • Deed restrictions, if approved by the property owner.
If reaching equipment performance limits, however, coincides with concentration declines in soil and/or groundwater to defined goals, then remediation is by definition fully complete.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: September 2015 18-63 Remediation Chapter 18: Remediation
Lessons Learned
September 2015
Introduction
This section contains “lessons learned” for designing and implementing a successful remedial action. These tips may not be valid for all types of remediation and are dependent on site conditions. It is recommended that the RP and/or consultant contact the lead regulatory agency for ideas and suggestions on how to execute a remedial action.
Explore Funding Sources

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Explore Funding Sources
The contamination at many sites is left un-remediated and may pose a risk to human health and the environment, due to the inability of RPs to fulfill the financial responsibility requirements for investigation and/or cleanup or, in some cases, a site has been abandoned. RPs may apply for funding opportunities through the California Underground Storage Tank Cleanup Fund. The UST Cleanup Fund chapter describes this process in greater detail. The RP and/or lead regulatory agency may also explore and apply for funding through the Emergency, Abatement, and Recalcitrant (EAR) Program, the Orphan Site Cleanup Fund Program, the Contamination Orphan Site Cleanup Subaccount Program, and the School District Account (Assembly Bill 2729). Please see the follow website for more information on these funding resources: http://www.swrcb.ca.gov/water_issues/programs/ustcf/ Immediate Source Area Removal

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
It is recommended to make every effort to conduct remedial activities (including over-excavation of soil) in the source area immediately after tank removal and not to postpone them until a full investigation, which can take years, is complete. It can be much cheaper, easier, and quicker to remediate the contamination immediately.
Plan According to Site–Specific Conditions
Understanding specific site conditions is imperative for the successful design and implementation of a remedial action. The following includes tips and methods for planning different types of site-specific conditions.
Continual Strategic Planning

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Continual Strategic Planning
When writing the first assessment work plan, it is recommended that the project manager assemble the geologists and remediation engineers to establish the list of data needs that can be collected with the first and each subsequent field assessment. For example, depending upon the soils encountered, various remediation technologies may be of limited use later in a project. Knowing this early in the project, the remediation engineers can steer the extra sampling needs toward technologies that may work with the site specific conditions present. After the data has been received from each assessment event, the team can re-assemble to reestablish future needs. This practice will maximize the budget of a project and effectiveness of a remediation.
During the feasibility study stage of the project, consider the entire problem and all potentially affected media; soil, groundwater, and soil vapor, and address them all when the first remediation system is installed. A “completed at the beginning of the project” approach can be the easiest way of ensuring that all elements of a site are included.
See the Conceptual Site Model chapter for more information.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
See the Conceptual Site Model chapter for more information.
Important! Know the end point (i.e., what are all the closure requirements and remediation goals?) when starting to design a remediation system. Then plan the design with a remediation technology or a series of remediation technologies that will efficiently reach those goals.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 18-64
Remediation
Avoid Risk of Contaminant Migration
Extraction wells and injection wells can be direct conduits to other aquifers and, if not sealed, can cause contamination to migrate from one aquifer to another. When designing a remediation system, always keep site-specific geology and hydrogeology in mind, including the location and depths of all aquifers when drilling.
Remedial Design Based on Site Conditions
UST are located almost everywhere, from remote locations that are only seasonably accessible to industrial properties to neighborhoods. Understanding the site-specific location characteristics is essential to implementing a successful site remediation. Issues to consider when implementing a remedial design in different types of locations include:
Light Pollution. Security lighting at a site may negatively impact the neighborhood. A possible solution to minimize light pollution is to use motion sensors or subdued lighting within the treatment compound.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Noise Pollution. Specifically for air-sparging and vapor-extraction systems, the compressors and blowers produce a lot of air and, if exhausted through too small a discharge pipe, will produce a very annoying whistle or whining noise.
Noise issues may disrupt neighbors. Several solutions include constructing a well-insulated structure to house the equipment, using noise blankets, and muffling or redirecting the discharge piping.
Discharge of Treated Groundwater via Infiltration Gallery. Knowing the local geology and infiltration rates is essential. There can be problems if water is discharged on the site and it daylights a few hundred feet away on an adjacent property.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Energy Source. Examine the availability of power – will a new electrical drop be needed, what voltage is available, will natural gas be needed, and what is the lead time for the utility? Before ordering equipment, contact the power company and request a written statement as to the voltage service with which the three-phase voltage systems will be connected to the system. If a three-phase, 230-volt service is assumed, and the equipment is ordered and installed to a three-phase, 208-volt service, the system will not work as designed and the equipment service life will be severely limited.
Understand the reliability of the power service in the vicinity and make preparations for re-start, where necessary.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Understand the reliability of the power service in the vicinity and make preparations for re-start, where necessary.
Power disruptions stop remediation, for example, in erratic winter weather. When a site is located in remote or rural areas and where weather can disrupt power for short time periods, the system may be off until a technician can return to restart the system, and weeks of remediation could be lost. In remote locations, such as in the Sierra Nevada, where self-generated power locations with routine maintenance on generators can cause disruptions in power, automatic restart functions can be designed to restart the system once power is restored.
Access Issues. Remote locations, for example, a cell tower near the crest of the Sierra Nevada, may be accessible for only 8 months per year to vehicular traffic. Other means of access will have to be considered in the operations and maintenance costs. Additionally, some LUFT sites are very small and may not be able to accommodate a large remediation system or the heavy machinery needed to install it.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text: Weather Conditions. With the decentralized operation of some firms, sometimes a remedial designer may be from another part of the country and may design the system based on knowledge of his or her own locale, and sometimes not be aware of site-specific conditions, including weather conditions. When designing a remediation system, the local weather conditions should be considered; for example, to winterize all exposed water piping, covering containment berms to avoid flooding equipment, or providing a new home or curiosity for unwanted fauna (bats, wasps, snakes, scorpions, rodents, bears, etc.)

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text: Permitting and Approvals. Determine all the permitting and approvals that may be needed to install and implement a remedial design. If water will be discharged, will the sanitation district need to approve the permit, or will a general waste discharge permit be required, and how long with this procedure take? Additionally, determine whether there are other agencies that may have input to the remedial design. Is there an architectural or planning committee that must approve your design to ensure that the housing or enclosure of the remedial system meets the architectural standards of the area?

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 18-65
Remediation
See the Health and Safety chapter for requirements and other issues that need to be considered and budgeted for working in the field.
Analysis of a Remediation System
Performance Criteria and Effectiveness
Prior to installation of a remediation system, estimate the performance criteria and cleanup schedule, so that when operational, the system can be evaluated (e.g., gallons of groundwater treated per day or pounds of petroleum vapor recovered per unit of time). This can be used to establish when the system will no longer be effective; for example, when influent concentrations have reached a point where the remediation technology is not cost-effective.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text: Sampling for Remediation Technology Selection and Potential Issues During the first round of assessment at a site, consider collecting additional, non-required data. Continuously core a minimum of two borings and log very carefully. This will provide information on whether the site has small seams of more permeable materials in the soil matrix or distinct zones of more permeable material, which will assist in designing the remedial system. Collect several core samples from distinct soil horizons and analyze for geotechnical properties, such as soil moisture, density, grain size, porosity, metal content, etc. Additionally, collect a minimum of one groundwater sample for water quality analysis (metals, hardness, alkalinity) and biological testing such as E. coli and coliform (if septic tanks are in the area). These tests will assist in the remediation technology selection and potential operation and maintenance issues later in the project.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text: Note. Revisiting and revising the CSM as new data become available is an effective way to continually analyze site conditions and remedial actions implemented. Communication and collaboration between the RP, consultant, and lead regulatory agency(ies) regarding the site status is imperative to maintain efficient and cost-effective remediation.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: September 2015 19-1
Remedial Optimization
Chapter 19: Remedial Optimization
September 2015
Scope of This Chapter
This chapter presents a summary of remedial optimization strategies for some common soil and groundwater remedies used at Leaking Underground Fuel Tank (LUFT) sites. All sites can benefit from optimization as it ensures remedial actions are preceding efficiently and effectively.
Remedial Optimization Benefits
The two main goals of remedial optimization are to reduce remediation time, in an effort to achieve timely site closure, and to reduce or limit remedial expenditures.
Additional benefits of remedial optimization efforts may include:
• Lower energy use
• Reduced carbon footprint
• Improved remedy protectiveness
• Improved project and site decision making
Senate Bill No. 445 (SB 445)
Optimization as a means of reducing remedial costs is of particular importance for sites in the Underground Storage Tank Cleanup Fund (UST Cleanup Fund). SB 445 limits the expenditure to $1 million for application to the UST Cleanup Fund after December 31, 2014. Previously, the cap was set at 1.5 million.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Definition. In the 2012 National Optimization Strategy, the USEPA defines optimization as, “Efforts at any phase of the removal or remedial response to identify and implement specific actions that improve the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of that phase. Such may also improve the remedy’s protectiveness and long-term implementation which may facilitate progress towards site completion.”
Basic Remedial Optimization Strategies
The overarching focus during the optimization process should be on moving the site towards closure. An exit strategy and end goals should be developed and the remedial technology needs to align with the strategy and goals for a LUFT site. Additionally, it is important to consider performance and cost during every step of the remedial optimization process. One of the most important steps in remedial optimization is the periodic review of system performance as this can help to identify adjustments needed to ensure the system is operating efficiently. These topics are covered more in-depth for each specific remedy in this chapter. Other topics include:

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• System Operations, including start-up and long term operation monitoring • Remedial progress, use of existing data to update the CSM and compare actual remedy performance to design expectation.
• Remedial system performance evaluation and troubleshooting, • System enhancement considerations
• Additional remedy-specific tools that can be used to help with remedial optimization.

California LUFT Manual: September 2015 19-2
Remedial Optimization
Important! Remedial Optimization needs to be considered at all times during the LUFT site assessment, remediation, and closure process stages.
Remedial Technologies Discussed
Optimization is discussed in detail in this chapter for the following remedial technologies. This discussion is not intended to include all of the remedial technologies available, but covers several of the most common remedial approaches at LUFT sites.
• Soil-Vapor Extraction
• Dual-Phase Extraction
• Long Term Groundwater Monitoring
• Air Sparging
• Biosparging
• In-Situ Chemical Oxidation

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-3
Remedial Optimization
Chapter 19: Remedial Optimization
Soil Vapor Extraction
December 2015
Soil Vapor Extraction (SVE) is the most used remediation technology for LUFT sites with volatile contaminants in the vadose zone. SVE is an attractive remediation approach because of the relatively simple installation and operation; it also typically requires a minimal amount of equipment. Additional information on the design and implementation of SVE at LUFT sites is presented in Chapter 18.
This section focuses on optimizing SVE remediation systems and discusses the following in terms of optimization:
• SVE System Operation optimization opportunities
• Conceptual Site Model (CSM) Data to be analyzed and evaluated to properly evaluate SVE system performance and optimization opportunities
• Analyzing, identifying, and quantifying remaining contaminant sources and how that data impacts decisions on optimization and remedial performance
• Decision logic to make determinations on SVE shutdown, optimization, enhancement, or transition into another technology.
• Additional SVE Enhancement opportunities
• Best Practices for SVE Optimization

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Best Practices for SVE Optimization
• Tools that Responsible Parties (RPs) and regulators can use for the SVE remedial optimization process SVE System Operation
Operating Cost Considerations
SVE operation objectives are to maximize mass removal with the existing extraction equipment until a point is reached where continued operation is no long cost effective. Since operating costs are fixed with respect to time, shorter operating periods result in lower total remediation costs. Roughly 50% of operating cost is driven by field visits by technicians required to monitor effluent treatment efficiency as defined by the air discharge permit.
Start-Up

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Start-Up
The initial operating period (a few days to a few weeks) should include systematic gathering and recording of system data and manifold valving adjustments. These adjustments should optimize contaminant mass removal by concentrating vacuum pressure on the extraction wells that are producing vapors with higher contaminant concentrations, thereby balancing flow and optimizing contaminant mass removal. During the start-up phase, flow measurements, vacuum readings, and vapor concentrations should be recorded daily from each extraction vent, from the manifold, and from the effluent stack (USEPA 2004).
Operation and Monitoring

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Operation and Monitoring
In terms of the operation and monitoring of SVE systems there are several considerations to keep in mind when thinking about optimization. Many inefficiencies with regard to the operation and monitoring of SVE and SVE with air sparging (AS) systems are related to the extraction and treatment of contaminant vapors. Below are some recommendations for optimizing the operation and monitoring of SVE systems and how to reduce unintended vapor emissions from USEPA’s Green Remediation Best Management Practice: Soil Vapor Extraction & Air Sparging Fact Sheet (USEPA 2010a).
• Consider adding a low-permeability soil cap at an area with negative pressure to prevent intrusion of clean air that can short circuit the extraction system.
• Make sure that the effective radius of influence (ROI) of vapor extraction wells completely covers the treatment area.
• Install and properly maintain surface seals around all wells and monitoring points, and routinely inspect to maintain a good seal.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-4
Remedial Optimization
• Maintain flow rates sufficient to prevent vapors from migrating beyond the treatment area without overloading the treatment system. Individually valved wells and dilution valves help simplify this process.
Well trained staff that can recognize and understand that a problem exists are imperative.
• Use vapor treatment methods appropriate for the influent vapor concentrations and change the method as treatment progresses. Additionally, selection of a vapor treatment method requires thorough understanding of the contaminants present at the Site. If chlorinated solvents are present, special precautions should be considered to prevent the production of hazardous waste in the exhaust stream and avoid damage to the treatment system.
• Regenerate adsorptive media such as GAC filters.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Regenerate adsorptive media such as GAC filters.
SVE Remedial and System Performance – Data to be analyzed and Evaluated To determine how and when to optimize an SVE system both the system performance and the remedial performance must be evaluated. Remedial performance refers to the progress towards meeting cleanup criteria and system performance refers to the degree to which a particular remedial component is meeting its design expectations (ITRC 2004). The remedial performance will be impacted by both the properties of the contaminants and the properties of the soil. The system performance will be impacted by system configuration and design limitations.
The process of data gathering and conducting evaluation on SVE performance provided below is primarily from Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Soil Vapor Extraction System Optimization, Transition, and Closure Guidance, 2013, reference document. This document provides a stepwise approach for information gathering and evaluating a SVE system. Below are items that should be considered when evaluating SVE system and remedial performance.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Revisit the design of the system and compare it to the current setup of the system at the site – Page 18-11 discusses effective ROI being the most important parameter to be considered in the design of an SVE system. It is important to make sure that the effective ROI of the system continues to completely cover the area of the current contamination, if remediation is still warranted (revisit CSM data to determine if the area of contamination has changed). Also, check to make sure that small components of the system aren’t damaged or missing.
• Update CSM information
• Remaining source location—where the bulk of remaining contaminant mass is relative to groundwater and surface receptors and details of the vadose zone source distribution (DOE 2013).
• Assessment of extent and magnitude of migration of contamination under natural conditions • Contaminant degradation and transformation data
• Environmental Impact Pathways and Receptors
• Site-specific “complicating factors” which are other variables that are site specific that can contribute to how contaminants migrate (e.g. large fluctuations in water table elevation because of seasonal variations).

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• See Section 2.0 of the DOE 2013 guidance document for additional suggestions on CSM information that should potentially be gathered as part of the evaluation.
• Analyze and identify remaining contaminant sources and impacts to groundwater. Answer specific questions that will help with the analysis of what contamination remains, where the contamination is coming from, and what are the impacts. A few questions from the DOE 2013 guidance document are presented below but there are several additional questions within the document.
• What is the mass discharge from the remaining sources under SVE operational conditions?
• What would the mass discharge be from the remaining sources if the SVE system were shut down?

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-5
Remedial Optimization
• What is the projected trend in mass recovery and mass discharge from the remaining sources over time for continued SVE operations?
• What is the dominant transport mechanism to the groundwater if the SVE system were shut down?
• Based on the source and mass discharge characteristics, where and how should the source be diminished to most readily meet goals?
• Quantify remaining contaminant sources and impacts to groundwater and compare to historical data.
DOE 2013 guidance document provides 4 steps for the quantification of contaminant sources. The steps are provided below.
• Step 1: Quantify the Vadose Zone Contaminant Source.
• Step 2: Estimate Impact to Groundwater
• Step 3: Estimate Impact to Vapor Intrusion

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Step 3: Estimate Impact to Vapor Intrusion
• Step 4: Estimate Impact of Source Decay, Sorption, and Attenuation Processes Note: When quantifying the vadose zone contaminant source (Step 1 above), high recharge sites might require alternative analyses that evaluates the role of vapor-phase and aqueous-phase contaminant transport. High recharge sites are sites with a recharge rate that is high enough to dominate contaminant transport from the vadose zone to groundwater. Appendix B of DOE 2013 provides guidance on how to analyze sites in which vapor and pore water are not in equilibrium.
SVE Remedial and System Performance – Decision Logic and Future Action Determinations
Determine future actions at the site using all the information gathered and use decision logic to make decisions on SVE shutdown, optimization, enhancement, or transition into another technology. Decision logic steps as presented in the DOE 2013 guidance document are provided below:
• Step 1: Make a determination if the SVE system can be terminated. Ask the question if the SVE system is terminated will the remediation goals be met?

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Step 1: Make a determination if the SVE system can be terminated. Ask the question if the SVE system is terminated will the remediation goals be met?
• Step 2: If the SVE system cannot be terminated, determine if the SVE system can be optimized to remove contaminant mass more efficiently and reach closure goals. Some considerations for optimization approaches:
• Focusing active extraction in areas that require significant mass removal, add passive/active air injection wells were air throughput is inadequate (location, depth, and screened interval), and terminating wells that are no longer needed. For complex sites consider using air flow modeling to help make decisions.
• Pulsing of the extraction system, which is periodic operation of active extraction and periods of no extraction, may achieve the same mass removal with lower operational costs. The period of inactivity will depend on the rate of diffusion and can be based on the amount of time concentrations rebound to some percentage (e.g., 60%) of a baseline concentration (USACE 2002).

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Passive extraction may be applicable at sites where there is a significant lag in subsurface pressure response to atmospheric pressure changes; the site stratigraphy must be appropriate and air permeability adequate to create air flow needed to remove/capture site mass flux.
• Coupling air injection (active or passive) with active extraction can improve air flow through zones with remaining mass while decreasing the applied vacuum and reducing water upwelling

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: September 2015 19-6
Remedial Optimization
• Supplementing SVE with dual-phase extraction (DPE) if the target mass is near the water table/capillary fringe.
• For sites with multiple extraction points, cycling a specific point off while increasing the flow rate to other extraction points may alter established subsurface flow pathways to potentially access additional contaminant mass.
AFCEE 2001, USACE 2002, and DOE 2013 were referenced for the above bullet points.
Important! The Low-Threat Underground Storage Tank Case Closure Policy (Policy) criteria should generate the remediation goals for a SVE system at most LUFT sites. The system should be designed and operated to meet the closure criteria defined in the Policy.
• Step 3: Sometimes SVE system termination and optimization are not viable options for continued remediation at a site. Alternative remediation strategies should also be considered as a next step after SVE system operation.
• The DOE 2013 guidance document breaks down alternatives into three categories of action for sites where the SVE operation has not been able to sufficiently diminish the vadose zone contamination.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• The DOE 2013 guidance document breaks down alternatives into three categories of action for sites where the SVE operation has not been able to sufficiently diminish the vadose zone contamination.
• Control contaminant flux from source to groundwater: consider alternative approaches such as infiltration barriers, passive SVE, oil injection at the water table, or use of active SVE periodically to control migration (P. 5.3).
• Control contaminant flux to the surface (VI issues): consider alternative approaches such as applying passive SVE, use of active SVE to control vapor migration, use of hydraulic or pneumatic fracturing with active or passive SVE to enhance capture, or active air injection to prevent vapor migration to sensitive surface areas. Additional information on technologies are provided in Section 5.2 of DOE 2013 guidance document.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Significant contaminant reduction required in the vadose zone: consider aggressive alternative approaches such as pneumatic/hydraulic fracturing of low-permeability zones with continued SVE, multi-phase extraction or air sparging (if the mass is primarily concentrated in high-moisture soils near the water table), and/or in-situ thermal remediation of the remaining low-permeability source zones. Additional information on technologies is provided in Section 5.2 of DOE 2013 guidance document.
• For sites that have contamination sources entering the vadose zone from groundwater the DOE 2013 guidance document breaks down alternatives into 2 categories.
• Control contaminant flux to the surface (VI issues): consider the same approaches as those listed in the 2nd bullet above.
• Contaminant reduction in the vadose zone: consider the same aggressive approaches presented in the third bullet above.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Contaminant reduction in the vadose zone: consider the same aggressive approaches presented in the third bullet above.
Fracturing: Pneumatic vs. Hydraulic? Pneumatic fracturing uses air or another gas to induce fracturing and is mostly utilized at sites with formations that allow for fractures to remain open without support while Hydraulic fracturing uses water or a water-based fluid to induce fractures. Both approaches may shorten the diffusion distance to paths where advective removal of contaminants can occur (EPA 1997).

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-7
Remedial Optimization
SVE Enhancements and Alternatives
The following list provides considerations for selecting SVE enhancements and alternatives and their applicability.
These are taken from the USEPA 1997 document:
• Excavate and treat contaminated soil ex situ, if the source is small and near the surface.
• Bioventing, if the source is amenable to aerobic bioremediation.
• Directional drilling should be considered as part of the remedial design of the SVE system and as an enhancement
• Apply pneumatic or hydraulic fracturing if the soil permeability is low (hydraulic conductivity of less than 10-6 centimeters per second [cm/s]).
• Apply thermal enhancement if the vapor pressures of the contaminant of concern are low (less than 0.5 mm Hg at ambient conditions), or where high soil moisture content prevents adequate air exchange.
• Apply DPE if light nonaqueous-phase liquid (LNAPL) is present or if the capillary fringe is targeted for cleanup.
• Air sparge to distribute oxygen in the groundwater and vadose zone and to induce bioremediation and contaminant stripping in groundwater if desired.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Air sparge to distribute oxygen in the groundwater and vadose zone and to induce bioremediation and contaminant stripping in groundwater if desired.
• In-situ chemical oxidation to reduce concentrations of petroleum hydrocarbons in groundwater.
For additional details on the above enhancements look at Chapters 3 through 7 of USEPA 1997 document.
Best Practices
The following Best Practices can be used when optimizing a SVE system.
• Regularly review data to ensure the design goals are being achieved and make adjustments to the system as needed. Milestones should be predicted in advance and shared with the field team.
• Consider using hand held gas detectors (e.g., PIDs and FIDs) as a field screening method to help determine if mass removal rates are reaching asymptotic limits. Field screening data can then be verified and calibrated periodically via analytical sampling. Make sure the analytical sampling frequency complies with air discharge permit requirements; some agencies may not accept field measurements.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Employ green remediation strategies when designing a SVE system to reduce total energy and reduce air pollutants, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and reduce water use. Ideas on green remediation strategies are provided in USEPA’s Green Remediation Best Management Practices Fact Sheet (USEPA 2010a).
• To help reduce a potential nuisance condition because of the noise levels from operating a SVE or SVE/AS system, consider using acoustic barriers, centrifugal blowers instead of positive displacement blowers, and installing airline mufflers (USEPA 2010a).

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-9
Remedial Optimization
Chapter 19: Remedial Optimization
Dual Phase Extraction
December 2015
Dual Phase Extraction (DPE), also referred to as Multi-Phase Extraction (MPE) and bioslurping, is a prevalent remediation approach for addressing LUFT sites. DPE is used to address volatile contaminants in groundwater and the vadose zone, as well as separate-phase product. DPE is an attractive remediation approach due to the generally short treatment times and applicability for a wide range of site conditions. Additional information on the application of DPE at LUFT sites is presented in Chapter 18.
This section focuses optimizing DPE remediation systems and discusses the following:
• Optimization opportunities during initial start-up and long term O&M of a DPE system • Evaluation of DPE Remedial Performance, including troubleshooting • Decision logic to make determinations on DPE shutdown, optimization, enhancement, or transition into another technology
• Additional DPE Enhancement opportunities
• Best Practices for DPE Optimization
• Tools that RPs and regulators can use for the DPE remedial optimization process DPE System Operation

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Tools that RPs and regulators can use for the DPE remedial optimization process DPE System Operation
In terms of the operation and monitoring (O&M) of DPE systems there are several considerations to keep in mind when thinking about optimization. Many of the O&M considerations for DPE systems have been covered as part of the O&M of SVE systems on pages 19-3 and 19-4. Below is some additional information to be considered during start-up and O&M of DPE systems.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text: • Initial start-up. There is typically a 7 to 10 day period of systematic gathering and recording of system data, adjustment of the vacuum pump settings and the depth of the extraction tube inlet for single-pump DPE systems, and a similar adjustment of the valves and pumps for the separate groundwater and air extraction systems of multi-pump systems. During the start-up adjustment period, flow measurements, pressure or vacuum readings, carbon dioxide concentrations, oxygen concentrations, and VOC concentrations should be recorded daily from each extraction well, from the manifold, and from the effluent stack. These measurements will be used to optimize the DPE system (USEPA 1995). For example, since the required applied vacuum to extract groundwater, LNAPL or soil gas from the soil cannot be precisely predicted during the design phase, the applied vacuum is typically increased gradually while monitoring to determine the ideal setting.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Long-term O&M. Long term monitoring should include flow-balancing, flow and pressure measurements, and vapor concentration readings. Measurements should be performed weekly or biweekly for the duration of system operation (USEPA 1995). Some common system optimization completed as part of typical O&M (USEPA 2009a):
• Adaptations to changes in water table, such as changes in pump depths, adjustments to drop tube depth, and alteration of applied vacuum and air flow.
• Installation of additional extraction wells and/or passive or active air injections wells.
• Well maintenance and/or rehabilitation to combat biofouling and solids in the extraction wells.
• Maintenance of equipment, such as blowers, pumps, and thermal oxidizers.
DPE Remedial and System Performance –System Evaluation, Troubleshooting When developing an optimization strategy for a remedial system both the DPE system performance and the remedial performance need to be evaluated. The process of gathering data and conducting evaluation on DPE

DPE Remedial and System Performance – Decision Logic and Future Action Determinations
Development of an exit strategy and an approach for site closure is an integral part of the design and implementation of the DPE system. Determine future actions at the site using all the information gathered in the previous steps and use decision logic to make decisions on DPE shutdown, optimization, enhancement, or transition into another technology. The total cost of DPE treatment and cost per kilogram mass removed over time should be plotted to assess the cost efficiency, which should be also be factored into the decision making process. Decision logic steps for DPE have been adapted from those provided for an SVE system in the U.S.
Department of Energy’s Soil Vapor Extraction System Optimization, Transition, and Closure Guidance (DOE 2013):
• Step 1: Make a determination if the DPE system can be terminated.
• System shutdown is typically performed when:

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• System shutdown is typically performed when:
• Remediation goals are reached. These goals are typically determined by the regulatory agency.
• The rate of mass removal is deemed not high enough to justify continued operation of the system. This is subjective and should be considered in the context of the original mass removal rates.
• Monitoring indicates air and groundwater removal rates have reached asymptotic levels.
• Step 2: If the DPE system cannot be terminated, determine if the system can be optimized to remove contaminant mass more efficiently and reach closure goals. Some considerations for optimization approaches:
• Drawdown/vacuum dewatering- enhances the effectiveness of vadose zone remediation and increases production of groundwater from low-yield aquifers.
• Downsize the DPE system- terminate wells that are no longer needed.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-12
Remedial Optimization
• Consider initiating system enhancements. Common DPE system enhancements and their applicability can be found in the DPE Enhancement Considerations section below.
• Step 3: Sometimes DPE system termination and optimization are not viable options for continued remediation at a site. Remedial alternatives should also be considered as a next step after DPE system operation. Some potential remedial alternatives include:
• SVE with Air Sparging- May be an appropriate remedial alternative if LNAPL is no longer present beneath the Site and the groundwater plume is not migrating offsite.
• Bioventing- At sites where the contaminants are primarily aerobically biodegradable, replacing active extraction with air injection would provide oxygen to the native bacteria and stimulate additional contaminant removal without the cost of off-gas treatment.
• Groundwater bioremediation- At sites where LNAPL has been removed and dissolved contamination is biodegradable. Can be combined with other remedial technologies such as air sparging, SVE, and bioventing.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Pump & Treat- Groundwater pump and treat is primarily used for plume containment.
DPE Enhancement Considerations
The following list provides considerations for selecting DPE enhancements and their applicability. These are taken from the USACE 1999 document:
• Excavate and treat contaminated soil ex situ, if the source is small and near the surface.
• Conventional LNAPL recovery, best suited for sites with homogeneous, coarse-grained soils where LNAPL will flow freely into a recovery well or trench.
• Vacuum dewatering lowers the water table, permitting the flow of air through previously saturated soil which allows VOCs to partition into the air stream and may enhance soil aeration and dissolved oxygen content of soil pore water, stimulating in-situ aerobic biodegradation.
• Vacuum-enhanced LNAPL recovery, helps to overcome capillary forces so that LNAPL can flow towards the extraction wells at sites with LNAPL present in the capillary fringe.
• Soil fracturing, may enhance effectiveness of the DPE system by creating additional high permeability pathways within otherwise low permeability strata, extending the effective ROI of extraction wells.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Thermal enhancement, increases vapor pressure and solubility of VOCs and SVOCs, increases air permeability by removing moisture.
• Air injection, increases subsurface pressure gradients which increases subsurface gas flow rates, eliminates stagnant zones, and, as a primary method of bioventing, increases aerobic biodegradation.
• Air sparge to distribute oxygen in the groundwater and vadose zone and to induce bioremediation and contaminant stripping in groundwater if desired.
• Surfactant/co-solvent flushing, alcohols or surfactants can enhance the rate of NAPL dissolution when added to groundwater in high concentrations (e.g., 50% by volume in the case of cosolvents).
• Pulsing of the system, which involves alternating periods of system operation and periods of system shutdown, may reduce operation costs. However, in many cases pulsed operation is less efficient than operating at a very low, sustained rate (USEPA 1995).
For additional details on the above enhancements look at Chapter 3 of the USACE 1999 document.

Usually, the groundwater monitoring network developed during the site characterization process is incorporated into the remedial phase of monitoring. Site characterization networks are usually unsuitable for LTM as they were set up for a different purpose i.e. to define the nature and extent of contamination when there were many unknowns about the site. This situation may lead to redundant or deficient monitoring. To correct the deficiencies, wells may have to be relocated and/or replaced. Optimizing the LTM program is expected to reduce the cost of the program as well as make it more effective.
Note: The main objective of conducting LTMO is to reduce the cost of monitoring without losing program effectiveness.

Another factor beyond the scope of this chapter but one that may substantially contribute to a reduction in overall LTM program cost is the optimization of the design and/or operation of the remedial system.
Documenting the Goals and Objectives of the LTM Program Before optimizing the LTM program, it is essential to define and document the goal(s)/objective(s) of the LTM at a site. This may be done through developing the groundwater monitoring plan (GMP) and then working to obtain stake-holders buy-in and regulator approval to implement it.

LTM Well Network
The monitoring points (types and location of wells) of the LTM program depends on the regulator approved GMP.

Upgradient wells are located away from the source of contamination in the direction from which groundwater flows. Concentrations in these wells represent contaminants flowing onto the site, if any. An uncontaminated upgradient well may be used as a background well.

Background wells are located where they cannot be affected by contamination. They are used to determine background concentrations of contaminants, usually metals or other naturally occurring compounds. An upgradient well may serve as a background well.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Crossgradient Crossgradient
Crossgradient wells are located adjacent to the source of contamination in a direction perpendicular to the direction of groundwater flow. These wells may be used to ensure that diffusion, dispersion, or seasonal variations in flow direction do not result in the additional spread of contamination from a site.
Plume-Edge Downgradient
or Crossgradient
Plume-edge wells are located immediately outside, and downgradient or crossgradient of a plume and are used to track plume movement by flow, diffusion, or dispersion. Wells designated as plume-edge wells may need to change as the plume size and shape change. These wells may be part of a remedial system.
In-Plume Downgradient
In-plume wells are located both vertically and horizontally within the known extent of Contamination or plume. These wells are used to track concentration changes over time.
These wells may also serve as extraction wells for a remedial system.
Downgradient Downgradient

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Downgradient Downgradient
Downgradient wells are located in the direction of groundwater flow from the source of contamination. Downgradient wells are used to track the concentration and movement of contaminants from a site. In-plume, plume-edge, and sentinel wells may all be downgradient wells.
Sentinel Downgradient
Sentinel wells are positioned downgradient of the contamination and upgradient of some sensitive receptor, such as a drinking water source. Sentinel wells must be screened at an interval appropriate to what they are protecting.

Remedial Optimization
Methods for Optimizing the Number, Spatial Distribution, and Sampling Frequency of Wells There are three optimization methods generally employed:
• Qualitative method that uses professional judgments to eliminate redundancies/deficiencies;
• Quantitative methods use statistics and geostatistics (spatial statistics) to evaluate redundancies/deficiencies),
• Combination (of qualitative and quantitative) approaches that employ the tool of decision criteria (need regulatory approval) to address redundancies/deficiencies.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Combination (of qualitative and quantitative) approaches that employ the tool of decision criteria (need regulatory approval) to address redundancies/deficiencies.
In order to assess the degree to which a site monitoring program is achieving the objective of tracking the time related contaminant change in concentration at a particular location (temporal objective), and the concentration changes at other monitoring locations (spatial objective), the LTMO evaluation needs to address the temporal and spatial characteristics of the groundwater quality data. Temporal and spatial data are most rigorously evaluated using temporal statistical and spatial statistical techniques (Quantitative Method). However, there may be other site considerations that may be best addressed through qualitative evaluation (Qualitative Method). In a qualitative evaluation, it is usually possible to consider numerous site factors simultaneously and then use the results of temporal or spatial statistical evaluations to support the results of a qualitative evaluation (Combination Method). There is thus no “one right way” of doing LTMO evaluations.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Optimizing the Number and Spatial Distribution of Monitoring Wells The types of wells and their spatial distribution at an LTM site are a function of the goals and objectives of the regulator-approved GMP. However, there may be more wells than necessary and some of these may not be deployed at the appropriate locations.
Geostatistics and temporal trend analysis are the appropriate statistical methods for this type of optimization.
Geostatistical methods are used to evaluate the spatial pattern and correlation of contamination across a region, allowing one to observe which locations continue to have unacceptably high concentrations. Regression analyses can identify trends (typically linear trends) by determining if the regression model provides a good fit and by identifying how strongly concentrations correlate with time.

Optimizing Monitoring Frequency and Duration
It is estimated that reducing monitoring frequency by 50% will decrease sampling labor, analysis, validation, and reporting costs by a like percentage. Decreasing the number of samples through reductions in sampling duration and/or frequency is therefore important to optimizing the existing LTM program.
The function of a well should be taken into account when determining the sampling frequency.
Downgradient, plume-edge wells generally require more frequent sampling than an upgradient or background well background well. Special purpose wells, such as sentinel wells, may need to be sampled often to safeguard human health.

Optimizing the Non-Physical Elements of LTM
The Data Quality Objective Process (DQO) may be used to optimize the suite of analytes, sampling and analytical methods. The purpose of the DQO process is to define the types and quality of data necessary to support the decisions to be made during the monitoring. DQOs therefore support the overall objective of the monitoring program. Please refer to the chapter on DQO for more information.
The tools that may be used to optimize data evaluation, data management, and reporting are the geographic information systems (GIS), statistical and geostatistical, custom databases, and graphical and tabular formats.
These tools can help summarize monitoring data, compare against decision criteria, and draw the appropriate conclusions about the data. These presentation tools also ensure that data interpretation and evaluation of decision criteria are clear and logical to interested parties.
Selecting the Right LTMO Candidate
The minimum conditions to meet are:

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
1. Number of monitoring points (wells); and
2. Total number of samples collected and analyzed per year (product of total number of wells, number of samples per well, and annual sampling frequency of each well).
Historical experience at large non LUFT sites (Roadmap to LTMO, 2005) shows:
1. The number of samples collected per year can be reduced from 10 to 50 percent when implementing the results of an LTMO evaluation of an existing program of moderate size (30 to 100 samples collected and analyzed per year). In addition to monitoring reductions, LTMO evaluation can potentially identify data deficiencies that may require additional new wells and/or sampling.
2. A qualitative LTMO evaluation of a moderate size program (20 to 30 monitoring points) may typically cost about $2,500. The cost of conducting a detailed LTMO evaluation of a larger program (> 30 monitoring points), using a combination of qualitative, temporal, and spatial approaches (expensive software) may cost about $25,000. Assuming a payback period of 3 years, cost savings of $800 to $8,300 per year must be realized for the LTMO evaluation to be cost effective.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
3. Assuming a cost range for sample collection and analysis of $200 per sample to $800 per sample, a LTMO evaluation that reduces the total number of samples collected at a site by about 5 to 15 samples should be cost effective.
4. If payback period of total up-front costs is more than several years (>3 years) then the changes to the monitoring program may not be appropriate.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-21
Remedial Optimization
LTMO Implementation Strategy for LUFT Sites
The May 19, 2009 State Water Resources Control Board Resolution No. 2009-0042 requires, in part, that all UST Cleanup Fund supported monitoring programs be operated on a semi-annual basis, unless the local regulatory agency directs otherwise. This monitoring frequency reduction has resulted in substantial monitoring cost reduction. Further reduction in monitoring cost for sites in LTM phase may be realized through the application of an appropriate and low cost LTMO methodology. The elements to consider in the preliminary development and implementation of this low cost approach are:

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Average LTM Size: This may be estimated from the product of average # of total wells for a typical site, number of samples per well, and sampling frequency per year per well. Using conservative numbers, this arithmetic works out to be (12)(3)(2) or 72 samples per year. [Using $300 per sample for collection/analysis, $90 per sample for reporting, the total yearly cost works out to be $28,000 or about $30,000 for the average size LTM]. By historical standards the average LTM size of 72 samples per year falls within the moderate size range. Cost savings may be realized if the cost of the LTMO is reasonable.
• Low Cost approach to LTMO: The monitoring program is of moderate size and the average number of wells (12) is low. Thus no expensive/sophisticated commercial software is needed for spatial and temporal analysis to compute the optimum number and placement of wells, or optimum monitoring frequencies. It appears that a primarily qualitative evaluation, supported when needed, by simple statistical tools (e.g. for trend analysis) should be adequate. Such an LTMO approach should not therefore be cost prohibitive.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• A pilot project consisting of one small and two moderate size LTMs should be selected for LTMO to see if the low cost LTMO approach is feasible.
• A Project Neutral Consultant/Contractor is recommended to do the LTMO evaluations and implement its recommendations (The regulator/UST Cleanup Fund staff could recommend GMP revisions to the contractor). The incumbent consultant/contractor may not have the incentive to conduct the LTMO and implement the recommendations. The UST Cleanup Fund could contract directly with an outside consultant to pay for a certain number of LTMOs per year if the pilot project is successful.

text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-22
Remedial Optimization
Chapter 19: Remedial Optimization
Air Sparging
December 2015
Air sparging is a remediation approach for addressing volatile contaminants in groundwater. Air sparging is an attractive remediation approach for groundwater treatment at LUFT sites because of the minimal costs as compared to other groundwater remediation technologies, such as groundwater pump and treat. Chapter 18 discusses the design and application of an air sparging systems at LUFT sites on pages 18-24 through 18-29.
This section focuses on optimizing air sparging remediation systems and discusses the following in terms of optimization:
• Optimization opportunities during initial start-up and long term O&M of an air sparging system • Evaluation of air sparging remedial performance, including troubleshooting • Decision logic to make determinations on air sparging shutdown, optimization, enhancement, or transition into another technology.
• Additional air sparging enhancement opportunities • Best Practices for air sparging Optimization

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Additional air sparging enhancement opportunities • Best Practices for air sparging Optimization
• Tools that RPs and regulators can use for the air sparging remedial optimization process Air Sparging and Soil Vapor Extraction
Air sparging (AS) is often paired with soil vapor extraction (SVE) for contaminant removal. Design optimization recommendations for AS/SVE systems are listed in the SVE System Design section on page 18-12.
Air Sparging System Operation
There are several considerations to keep in mind when thinking about optimization of the operation and monitoring (O&M) of an air sparging system. The three most significant factors affecting air sparging performance are (Leeson et al. 2002):
• The air distribution in the target treatment zone • The distribution (location and concentration) of contaminants relative to the air distribution • The contaminant characteristics (composition and chemical properties)
Startup Operations

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Startup Operations
Objectives of the startup operations include optimizing equipment operation, systematic gathering and recording of baseline data, and adjustments of operating parameters. If SVE will be used, the startup phase should begin with only the SVE portion of the system, as described in the SVE section of Chapter 18. Once the SVE system is adjusted, the air sparging system should be started. There is typically a 7 to 10 day period of manifold valving adjustments to balance injection rates and optimize mass flow rates. Injection and extraction rates, pressures, depth to groundwater, hydraulic gradient, and VOC levels should be recorded hourly during initial startup until the flow is stabilized. Once flow is stabilized, injection rates should be monitored daily. Vapor concentration should also be monitored in any nearby utility lines, basements, or other subsurface confined spaces (USEPA 1994a).
The following issues should be addressed during the design, startup, and/or optimization phases in order to ease transition of the system to final shutdown (NAVFAC 2001b):

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
The following issues should be addressed during the design, startup, and/or optimization phases in order to ease transition of the system to final shutdown (NAVFAC 2001b):
Placement of sparging wells. Focus placement of sparging wells in areas of elevated contaminant concentrations or the plume centerline. This will result in reduced cost of installation, as compared to complete plume coverage, without a substantial increase in operating time.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-23
Remedial Optimization
Reduce equipment capacities. Reduce the design capacity of air supply, vapor extraction, and vapor treatment units. Although this will reduce the maximum mass removal capacity of the system, it will ensure the system operates near its optimum design capacity (60 to 80% of maximum capacity) for a longer duration.
While this will result in lower capital equipment expenses, reducing maximum removal capacity may result in extended remediation time; this possibility should be evaluated.
Mobile equipment. Consider constructing air supply, vapor extraction, and vapor treatment units on mobile trailers. This may reduce the fixed costs of equipment and enable the equipment to be reused at other sites.
Furthermore, air supply and extraction equipment may be used for additional remediation activities, beyond air sparging and soil vapor extraction.
Long-Term O&M

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
Long-Term O&M
Long-term monitoring should include contaminant level measurements (in the groundwater, vapor wells, and blower exhaust), flow-balancing (including flow and pressure measurements), and vapor concentration readings, taken at bi-weekly to monthly intervals for the duration of the system operation. Periodic remedial system evaluation can help identify system modifications, such as adjustment of airflow rates or pulsing, to increase performance and efficiency.
Samples collected during sparging operations may report contaminant concentrations lower than those in surrounding aquifers. Additional samples should be collected following system shutdown, when the subsurface environment has reached equilibrium, to confirm remediation goals have been achieved (USEPA 1994a).

Air Sparging Remedial and System Performance – Decision Logic and Future Action Determinations
Development of an exit strategy and an approach to site closure is an important part of the design and implementation of the air sparging system. Determine future actions at the site using all the information gathered and use decision logic to make decisions on system shutdown, optimization, enhancement, or transition into another technology. Decision logic steps include:
• Step 1: Determine if the air sparge system can be terminated. System shutdown should be considered if:
• The remaining concentrations in groundwater are at or below the remediation goals.
• There is minimal rebound.
• The system has reached an asymptotic level of mass removal.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-25
Remedial Optimization
Note: As part of the exit strategy, the air sparging system should remain in place for at least one year after system shutdown in case contaminant rebound requires additional operation (NAVFAC 2001b).
• Step 2: If the system cannot be terminated, determine if the system can be optimized to remove contaminant mass more efficiently and reach closure goals. Some considerations for optimization approaches (NAVFAC 2001b):
• Optimize airflow to maximize mass removal. Mass removal is maximized in homogeneous deposits by uniform distribution within the treatment area corresponding to the distribution of contaminants. In heterogeneous deposits, focusing sparging activities in areas of greater permeability is likely to be an efficient way to maximize removal.
• Optimize well placement by focus air sparging and extraction in areas with highest contaminant concentrations. This may require adding wells in some areas and removing or shutting off wells in other areas.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Consider initiating system enhancements. Common air sparging system enhancements and their applicability can be found in the DPE Enhancement Considerations section below.
For additional information on the above system optimizations, see Chapter 5 of the NAVFAC 2001 Air Sparging Guidance Document.
• Step 3: Consider alternatives as the next step following air sparging. Some potential remedial alternatives include:
• Monitored natural attenuation
• Chemical oxidation
• Groundwater pump and treat
• Dual phase extraction
Air Sparging Enhancement Considerations
The following list provides considerations for selecting air sparging enhancements. These are taken from the USEPA 1997, USEPA 2009, and USACE 2013 documents:
• Excavate and treat contaminated soil ex situ, if the source is small and near the surface.
• SVE for contaminant removal.
• Injections of other gases such as:
• Ozone or oxygen to increase availability of oxygen for biodegradation.
• Methane or propane as co-metabolites.
• Nitrogen to reduce the formation of ferric oxide in the pore spaces of aquifers with high iron concentrations.
• Groundwater recirculation wells to increase the treatment zone.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
• Groundwater recirculation wells to increase the treatment zone.
• Cycling or pulsing the air flow during air sparging to increase mixing in the saturated zone, thus increasing volatilization and biodegradation of contaminants. For sites using AS/SVE with multiple extraction points, cycling one point off while increasing the flow rate to other extraction points may alter established subsurface flow pathways to potentially access additional contaminant mass.
• Thermal enhancements - hot air or steam can be injected to increase phase-change and diffusion rates of contaminants.

title: LUFT Manual (Leaking Underground Fuel Tank Guidance Manual)
text:
California LUFT Manual: December 2015 19-26
Remedial Optimization
• Supplemental injection of nutrients to enhance biodegradation.
Best Practices
The following Best Practices can be used when optimizing an air sparging system.
• Consistent system monitoring and as needed adjustments will help retain system efficiency.
• Consider green remediation strategies when designing an air sparging or AS/SVE system to reduce total energy and reduce air pollutants, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and reduce water use. Ideas on green remediation strategies are provided in USEPA’s Green Remediation Best Management Practices Fact Sheet (USEPA 2010a).
